question: In how many of the 12 settings do agents beat the strongest human-engineered SSL baselines, and by up to how much?

results.text: We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%.

9 Discussion and Conclusion

We introduced AgentSSL, which formulates semi-supervised learning as agentic program search. Under label scarcity, MLE agents generate SSL programs that beat tuned human baselines in 8 of 12 settings when the best program is known, but neither agents nor human pipelines can reliably pick that program without labels.

• We show that MLE agents can autonomously discover diverse, domain-adapted SSL programs that effectively leverage unlabeled data, achieving performance competitive with established SSL baselines, outperforming them in 8 of 12 settings.

question: Into which two sub-problems do the authors split the task of applying SSL with agents?

results.text: We decompose this problem into two core challenges:(1) program discovery, where agents must discover effective SSL programs under limited feedback, and(2) program selection, where a single program must be identified from the discovered candidates without a large labeled validation set.

We formulate AgentSSL as an agentic search problem over the space of SSL programs, comprising two core challenges:(1) program discovery, where an agent iteratively generates and refines candidate programs under limited feedback, and(2) program selection, where a single program must be identified from the discovered candidates for deployment under l

More broadly, we view the defining challenge of AgentSSL, and of the practical application of SSL more generally, as searching for effective programs in a regime with little or no validation data. Whether and how to leverage unlabeled data is therefore itself part of the search problem.

question: What does oracle performance measure when assessing program discovery?

results.text: Evaluation. We evaluate these two challenges separately. To assess program discovery, we measure oracle performance, defined as the test performance of the best program in the discovered pool, Q(A∗). This measures the quality of the best discovered solution, independent of our ability to select it.

5 Results

Across datasets and shot settings, AgentSSL discovers programs that are competitive with strong SSL baselines when programs are selected using oracle test performance (Table 1).

The gap between oracle and practical selection, however, highlights a central challenge for AgentSSL and SSL more broadly:identifying the best discovered program when validation feedback is weak. Table 2 reports practical selection regret when using the feedback metric for selection.

question: How long does each agent run last on the smaller datasets (DTD, RESISC45, KITTI), and on which GPU?

results.text: For the smaller datasets, DTD, RESISC45, and KITTI, we run each agent for 8 hours on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation GPU. For a comparison between baseline and agent compute costs, see Appendix B.2.

A.3 Total Compute

We scale the agent search budget according to the computational cost of the corresponding SSL baselines, since candidate evaluation time increases substantially with dataset size. For the smaller datasets (DTD, RESISC45, and KITTI), each agent run is allocated 8 GPU hours on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation GPU.

Across 6 datasets, 2 shot settings, and 3 random seeds, each agent setting comprises 36 runs: 18 with an 8-hour budget and 18 with a 15-hour budget. We evaluate two agent settings, unsupervised and noisy validation, for a total compute budget of 2×(18×8 + 18×15) = 828 GPU hours.

question: Under what condition is it better to spend labels on program selection rather than on training?

results.text: We also introducedProgramSelectBench(Appendix C), which makes this selection problem measurable, and our results show that when unsupervised metrics fail, labels spent on selection buy more accuracy than the same labels spent on training.

First, we find that unsupervised metrics enable effective selection when underlying assumptions hold. Second, when unsupervised metrics fail, actively allocating labels to program selection can outperform allocating them to training.

When unsupervised metrics fail, active model selection offers a promising alternative by using labels for selection. Under a fixed budget, we compare training on all labels with unsupervised selection against splitting labels evenly between training and active selection (Table 3).
